extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and PR professionals seeking background on McDonald's
extracted.subtask_description: Comprehensive Wikipedia-style corporate profile of McDonald's covering history, marketing, labor, legal cases, nutrition, animal welfare, charity, and future plans; useful as background for press releases or PR research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency campaign — 'Our Food. Your Questions.'
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's USA launched the 'Our Food. Your Questions.' transparency campaign, inviting customers to submit questions online, and published behind-the-scenes videos and other content about its ingredients, sourcing, and food preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign included a series of online videos featuring former MythBusters co-host Grant Imahara visiting suppliers and facilities. Presented as a PR/engagement tactic to address criticism and increase transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutritional reformulation (removal of trans fats and ingredient changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to public pressure McDonald's announced in May 2008 that, in the United States and Canada, it switched to using cooking oil that contains no trans fats for its french fries, and canola-based oil with corn and soy oils for its baked items, pies, and cookies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes are presented as reactive measures to health criticism (e.g., Super Size Me) and part of menu/ingredient reformulation and nutrition-focused PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing to children (playgrounds, games, toys, Happy Meals)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's uses playgrounds, games, and toys to make children want to go to McDonald's; children's advertising is a major part of the brand (see Ronald McDonald and McDonaldland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is noted both as a core marketing strategy and a frequent target of criticism for advertising targeted at children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity endorsements and co-branded meals
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's has used celebrity endorsements and partnerships (examples: Michael Jordan 'McJordan', LeBron James, Travis Scott Meal, J Balvin Meal, BTS Meal, Angel Reese Special) to promote exclusive menu items and merchandise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorsements have included exclusive or themed menu items, uniform/merch collaborations, and can generate high-profile media attention and sales spikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsorship strategy (sporting events, broadcast-centered advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's sponsors sporting events ranging from Little League to the FIFA World Cup and Olympic Games and has long used television as a central channel in its advertising strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsorship and broad-media presence are core to brand strategy; sponsorships (e.g., NASCAR) have been long-term tactical choices to reach target audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal welfare commitments (cage-free eggs and poultry welfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's pledged to stop using eggs from battery cage facilities in restaurants in Australia by 2017 (met in 2018) and faced criticism for use of fast-growing chicken breeds that raise welfare concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because McDonald's purchases large volumes of eggs (over 2 billion per year), supplier commitments (e.g., cage-free eggs) are positioned as having industry-wide impact; such pledges are part of responding to animal welfare advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark enforcement practices and risks ('Mc'/'Mac' disputes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The company has threatened many food businesses with legal action unless they drop the 'Mc' or 'Mac' from trading names; EUIPO and later ECJ rulings illustrate legal limits and reputational risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive trademark enforcement can provoke competitive trolling (e.g., Burger King responses), EUIPO cancellations for lack of genuine use, and adverse publicity; legal outcomes (Big Mac trademark narrowed to beef burgers) demonstrate enforcement limits and PR consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment contract policies (use of zero-hour contracts and shift to fixed contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2013, 90% of McDonald's UK workforce were on zero-hour contracts; after labor strikes in April 2017, employees were given the option of fixed contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting practices are a source of labor criticism and organizing (strikes); contract policy changes can follow industrial action and affect public perception and workforce stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace harassment, discrimination, and compliance measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports (e.g., BBC investigation) allege a toxic culture of sexual assault, harassment, racism and bullying at UK outlets; company instituted anti-harassment training, dismissed some workers for sexual harassment, and set up a specialist investigative unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale allegations lead to legal claims, regulatory attention (e.g., Equality and Human Rights Commission letters requiring compliance or risk of enforcement), and require organizational responses (training, investigations, policy changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product safety and liability (hot coffee / service practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liebeck v. McDonald's Restaurants (1994) examined McDonald's practice of serving coffee so hot that spills caused third-degree burns and resulted in a multimillion-dollar award (later reduced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product-service practices that create physical harm carry major liability and PR risk; legal outcomes can influence product-temperature policies and warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchisee compliance risk (child labor and wage-hour violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations by the United States Department of Labor found child labor violations at McDonald's franchises (e.g., over 300 children in Kentucky), resulting in fines against specific franchises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate reputation can be harmed by franchisee noncompliance; central company may face scrutiny though enforcement targets are often franchisees; monitoring and franchise compliance programs are implied mitigation tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate charitable activities (McHappy Day and Ronald McDonald House Charities)
rubrics_metrics.description: McHappy Day is an annual event during which a percentage of the day's sales go to charity; Ronald McDonald House Charities (RMHC) is a global network providing family support, with hundreds of chapters and large donation amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charitable programs are significant elements of corporate social responsibility and PR, with measurable fundraising outcomes and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and sustainability commitments (deforestation elimination, net-zero target)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's committed to eliminating deforestation from its global supply chain by 2030 for beef and four other commodities and has a 2050 net-zero carbon emissions commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit time-bound sustainability targets tied to supply-chain sourcing; they serve as public commitments that stakeholders will track and hold the company accountable for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital transformation and measurable targets (Digitizing the Arches, loyalty and digital ordering goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiatives include 'Digitizing the Arches' with a partnership with Google to automate restaurants using AI and Google Cloud; targets include expanding loyalty program active users from 150 million to 250 million by 2027 and increasing app-originated deliveries to 30% by 2027.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital/automation initiatives are framed with concrete numeric goals and vendor partnerships, reflecting priorities for operational change and growth metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menu/product changes in response to criticism (removing Super Size, introducing adult Happy Meal, McPlant, ingredient removals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following criticism (e.g., Super Size Me), McDonald's eliminated the super size option and created an adult Happy Meal; it also tested/introduced plant-based options (McPlant) and removed certain artificial preservatives and ingredients from some products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Menu adjustments and new product introductions are positioned as responses to health/consumer pressure and can be used defensively to address reputational issues and capture new market segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of litigating critics — the McLibel precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: In the McLibel case McDonald's sued activists for distributing critical leaflets; the long-running trial and European Court of Human Rights finding that unequal resources breached defendants' free-speech rights was widely seen as a 'PR disaster' for McDonald's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing libel/legal action against critics can produce prolonged legal exposure and backfire in public perception; the case is cited as an example of litigation harming reputation.
